title: Test it: a test plan for every button and every box, with evidence and a retest log
kind: a testing chapter: it earns AO1, AO2 and AO3 marks
one: You write a test plan that tries every button, link and menu item on every form, and every rule on every box. Then you run each test in Visual Studio 2019, keep a screenshot for each one, fix what fails and test it again.

stages.title: Plan a test for every way to move between forms

screens.title: Set up your test plan as a table

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will have an empty test plan table in your portfolio, with the right columns.
A [[test plan|0]] is a table of every test you will run, written before you run any of them.
The marker gives top marks only to a plan that tests every way to move between forms and all the data a player types in. A plan that misses some of either gets fewer marks.

words: A table of every test you will run on your game, written before you run them.
Data that follows the rule, so the game must allow it, such as `ridgeRunner` as a username.
Data that breaks the rule, so the game must refuse it with a message, such as `ridge!`.
Data right on the edge of a rule, or one step past it, such as a username of exactly 12 characters.
Data far past the edge of a rule, such as a username of 30 characters, to check the game copes.
A screenshot that shows a test being run and what the game did.
Running a failed test again after you fix the code, to show the fix works.
blocks.intro: You do not need to learn these words now. Where you first meet each one in the chapter, it has a dotted line under it. Hover over it or tap it to see what it means.

steps.see: Your browser shows that `test-plan-template.docx` has downloaded. Open it in Word and save it in your portfolio folder.

blocks.p: The template holds a table with 6 columns, in this order:

box.title: The 6 columns of your test plan

blocks.p: **Test number**: T1, T2, T3 and so on.
**What is tested**: the button, link, menu item or box, and the form it is on.
**Input**: what you click or type. Write typed data exactly, such as `abc12`.
**Expected result**: what must happen, written before you run the test.
**Actual result**: what did happen. Fill this in when you run the test.
**Screenshot number**: the number of the screenshot that shows it, such as S14.
The same table is your list of evidence. The marker reads a row, then finds its screenshot by the number.

screens.title: Write a row for every button, link and menu item

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, your test plan will have one row for each button, link and menu item on every form.
Open your navigation map from chapter 1. Each arrow on it is at least one row in your test plan.
Then go through your storyboard one form at a time. Add a row for every button, link and menu item that the map missed.

box.title: An example to read: navigation rows for the Summit Ready Log in and Welcome forms

blocks.p: **T1.** Log in form, **Register a new player** link. Click it. Expected: the Register form opens.
**T2.** Register form, **Back to log in** button. Click it. Expected: the Log in form shows again.
**T3.** Log in form, Help menu, **How to play**. Click it. Expected: a message says how to play the game.
**T4.** Log in form, Help menu, **About Summit Ready**. Click it. Expected: a message names the game and its credits.
**T5.** Log in form, File menu, **Exit**. Click it. Expected: the game closes.
**T6.** Welcome form, **Start the expedition** button. Click it. Expected: the map opens.
**T7.** Welcome form, Game menu, **Log out**. Click it, then click **Yes**. Expected: the Log in form shows again.
**T8.** Welcome form, Game menu, **Log out**. Click it, then click **No**. Expected: the Welcome form stays open.
A button that asks a question, such as **Log out**, needs a row for each answer. T7 and T8 are both needed.
In Summit Ready, the map has 8 summits, so it needs 8 rows: one row for each summit, opening its own game.
Each game also needs a row for **Back to the map**, and a row for its sound button.
Do not forget the window's own close button, the X at the top right. It is a way to leave a form too.

stages.title: Plan a test for every rule on every box

screens.title: Test every rule with 4 kinds of data

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know the 4 kinds of test data, and which ones each rule needs.
Every box a player types in has rules, and each rule needs its own rows in your test plan.
Test each rule with [[valid data|1]], [[invalid data|2]], [[boundary data|3]] and [[extreme data|4]].
A rule with an edge, such as a length from 3 to 12, has 2 edges to test. Test right on each edge, and one step past it.

box.title: An example to read: the 4 kinds of data for the Summit Ready username, which must be 3 to 12 characters

blocks.p: **Valid:** `ridgeRunner`. Expected: allowed.
**Invalid:** `ridge!`. Expected: refused with "Your username can only use letters and numbers. Take out the !."
**Invalid:** `ridge runner`. Expected: refused with "Your username can only use letters and numbers. Take out the space."
**Invalid:** a blank box. Expected: refused with "Type a username."
**Boundary:** `abc`, with 3 characters, and `abcdefghijkl`, with 12 characters. Expected: both allowed.
**Boundary:** `ab`, with 2 characters. Expected: refused with "Your username has 2 characters. It needs 3 to 12."
**Boundary:** `abcdefghijklm`, with 13 characters. Expected: refused with "Your username has 13 characters. It needs 3 to 12."
**Extreme:** a username of 30 letters. Expected: refused with the length message, and the game does not crash.
**Invalid:** `RIDGERUNNER`, when `ridgeRunner` is already a player. Expected: refused with "The username RIDGERUNNER is already taken. Try another one."
Write each expected message exactly as your game shows it. Then the actual result can be checked word for word.

screens.title: Test every password rule, and the log in form

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, your test plan will test every rule on the Register and Log in forms.

box.title: An example to read: the Summit Ready password rows, where a password must be 6 to 20 characters

blocks.p: **Valid:** `summit42`. Expected: allowed.
**Boundary:** `abc12`, with 5 characters. Expected: refused with "Your password needs 6 to 20 characters."
**Boundary:** `abc123`, with 6 characters. Expected: allowed.
**Boundary:** a password of 20 characters with a letter and a number. Expected: allowed.
**Boundary:** a password of 21 characters. Expected: refused with "Your password needs 6 to 20 characters."
**Invalid:** `abcdef`, with no number, and `123456`, with no letter. Expected: both refused with "Your password needs at least one letter and one number."
**Invalid:** `abc|123`. Expected: refused with "Your password cannot use the | character."
**Invalid:** a different password in the second box. Expected: refused with "The two passwords are different. Type them both again."
**Invalid:** no avatar clicked. Expected: refused with "Click a picture to choose your avatar."

box.title: An example to read: the Summit Ready Log in rows

blocks.p: **Valid:** `ridgeRunner` and `summit42`. Expected: the Welcome form opens.
**Valid:** `RIDGERUNNER` and `summit42`. Expected: the Welcome form opens, because a username may use any capitals.
**Invalid:** `ridgeRunner` and `Summit42`. Expected: refused, because a password must match exactly.
**Invalid:** a wrong password 3 times in a row. Expected: "Three wrong tries. Wait 30 seconds, then try again." The button counts down.
Your game may have different boxes. The rule is the same: every box, every rule, all 4 kinds of data.

screens.title: Test the boxes inside your games

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, your test plan will test the boxes and keys a player uses inside each game.
A game that asks the player to type, such as Grid Ref Rescue or Whiteout, has rules too.

box.title: An example to read: rows for the Grid Ref Rescue box and the Whiteout letters

blocks.p: **Valid:** `3127` in the Grid Ref box. Expected: allowed, and marked right or wrong.
**Invalid:** `31a7`. Expected: refused with "A grid reference here is four numbers, like 3127: two from the top of the map, then two from the left side."
**Boundary:** `312`, with 3 numbers. Expected: refused with the same message.
**Invalid:** `3940`, which is not on the map. Expected: refused with "3940 is not on this map." and the numbers the map uses.
**Invalid:** pressing E twice in Whiteout. Expected: "You have already tried E. Pick another letter."
None of these refusals costs the player any points. A badly typed grid reference is a typing problem, not a wrong answer.
Say so in your expected result, such as "Refused. The score stays the same." The marker rewards a game that knows the difference.
Add rows for the answers in each game too: a right answer, a wrong answer, and the score at the end of a round.

stages.title: Run your tests, keep the evidence, and fix what fails

screens.title: Run each test and keep a screenshot of it

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, every row of your test plan will have an actual result and a screenshot.
Run your game from Visual Studio 2019, then work down your test plan one row at a time.

steps.do: Do what the row says, such as type `ab` in the Username box and click **Create my player**.
steps.see: The game allows it or refuses it.

img.alt: The running Register form with ab typed in the Username box and the length message under it

marks.say: Do what the row says, such as type `ab` in the Username box and click **Create my player**.

steps.do: Press the Windows key, Shift and S together, then drag a box around the form.
steps.see: The screen goes grey while you drag. When you let go, the picture is copied.

steps.do: Paste the picture into your portfolio, under a heading with its screenshot number, such as S14.
steps.see: The picture shows the form, the data you typed, and the message the game showed.

steps.do: Write what happened in the Actual result column of the row.
steps.see: The row has its actual result and its screenshot number.

blocks.p: Each screenshot is [[evidence|5]]. It must show the data you typed and what the game did, both in the same picture.
A screenshot of a message alone does not prove which data caused it. Keep the box in the picture too.

screens.title: Keep a log of each fix and each retest

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will have a fix-and-retest log for every test that failed.
A test fails when the actual result is not the expected result. That is useful: it is a fault you found before the marker did.
Keep a second table, your fix-and-retest log, with 4 columns: test number, what went wrong, what you changed, and the [[retest|6]] result.

box.title: An example to read: two real fixes from the Summit Ready walk-through

blocks.p: **T12 failed.** After a wrong log in, the old error message was still there when the player came back to the Log in form.
**The fix:** the Log in form clears its error message each time it shows. **Retest:** passed, with a new screenshot.
**T41 failed.** In Whiteout, a letter already tried looked the same as a new one, so players pressed it again.
**The fix:** each tried letter now turns grey. **Retest:** passed, with a new screenshot.
Keep the screenshot of the failed test, as well as the retest. The pair shows the marker what you found and what you did.
Never change an expected result to match what went wrong. Fix the game, then test it again.
By the end of this screen, you will have written the analysis of your testing, which earns AO3 marks.
The analysis is a short section after your test plan. It says what your testing showed, not only which tests passed.

box.title: Answer these 4 questions in full sentences

blocks.p: How many tests did you run, and how many passed the first time?
Which tests failed, and why did each one fail?
What did you change, and did the retest pass?
What does your testing show about how well your game copes with bad data?
Name the rule and the test number each time, such as "T23 showed that a username of 13 characters was refused."
Run each check below on your test plan before you go on to chapter 20.

check.what: Every button, link and menu item on every form has a row.
check.how: Tick off each control on your storyboard as you find its row. Every control is ticked.

check.what: Every rule on every box has valid, invalid, boundary and extreme rows.
check.how: For each box, find a row of each of the 4 kinds of data.

check.what: The username `ab` in your own game.
check.how: Type it in your Register form, if your game has one, and click the button that saves the player.
check.fix: Go back to the chapter where you wrote that rule, and check the code that tests the length.

check.what: Every row has an actual result and a screenshot number.
check.how: Read down the last 2 columns. No cell is empty.

check.what: Every failed test has a row in your fix-and-retest log.
check.how: Find each failed row in the test plan, then find it in the log with its retest result.

blocks.p: Your portfolio now holds your test plan, a numbered screenshot for every row, your fix-and-retest log, and your analysis.
These give AO1 marks for the plan, AO2 marks for the screenshots, and AO3 marks for the analysis.
